Continuous Outcome: Communities and Crime Data

We will predict violent crime rate using socioeconomic predictors with the Communities and Crime dataset.

df <- read_csv("communities+and+crime/communities.data", col_names = FALSE, na = "?")

names(df) <- c("state","county", "community","communityname", "fold","population", "householdsize","racepctblack", "racePctWhite","racePctAsian", "racePctHisp","agePct12t21", "agePct12t29","agePct16t24", "agePct65up","numbUrban", "pctUrban","medIncome", "pctWWage","pctWFarmSelf", "pctWInvInc","pctWSocSec", "pctWPubAsst","pctWRetire", "medFamInc","perCapInc", "PctEmploy","PctEmplManu", "PctEmplProfServ","PctOccupManu", "PctOccupMgmtProf","MalePctDivorce", "MalePctNevMarr","FemalePctDiv", "TotalPctDiv","PersPerFam", "PctFam2Par","PctKids2Par", "PctYoungKids2Par","PctTeen2Par", "PctWorkMomYoungKids","PctWorkMom", "NumIlleg","PctIlleg", "NumImmig","PctImmigRecent", "PctImmigRec5","PctImmigRec8", "PctImmigRec10","PctRecentImmig", df_nomiss <- df %>% 
  select(-c(state:fold,LemasSwornFT:PolicAveOTWorked, PolicCars:LemasGangUnitDeploy, PolicBudgPerPop)) %>% 
  filter(complete.cases(.))

head(df_nomiss)

Distribution of outcome by candidate predictors

ggplot(df_nomiss, aes(x = PctIlleg, y = ViolentCrimesPerPop)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  labs(title = "Outcome distribution by house hold size")

ggplot(df_nomiss, aes(x = PctFam2Par, y = ViolentCrimesPerPop)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  labs(title = "Outcome vs. Median Income")

Fit CART with cross-validation to select CP

set.seed(735)

fit.n <- rpart(ViolentCrimesPerPop~., 
               data=df_nomiss, 
               method="anova", 
               control = list(minbucket = 5, 
                              cp = 0.0000002, 
                              xval = 50))

Fit_table.n <- as.data.frame(fit.n$cptable)
kbl2(Fit_table.n, caption = "50-Fold CV Results for CART (minbucket = 5)")

     xlab = "Number of splits",ylab="CV error",
     main = "CV error by number of splits",
     type = "l", xlim=c(0,min(c(max(Fit_table.n$nsplit),100))))

Best_mod <- which.min(Fit_table.n$xerror)
Best_mod_1sd <- which.max(Fit_table.n$xerror < c(Fit_table.n$xerror+Fit_table.n$xstd) [which.min(Fit_table.n$xerror)])
abline(v = Fit_table.n$nsplit[Best_mod] ,lwd=3)
abline(v = Fit_table.n$nsplit[Best_mod_1sd], lwd = 3, col = 4)

Final tree

Here, we’ll use the 1-sd criteria to get our final tree:

j <- Best_mod_1sd
kbl2(Fit_table.n[j,])
CP nsplit rel error xerror xstd
5 0.0195108 4 0.4332585 0.4503099 0.0216111 
# Get Cp for the best model
cp <- Fit_table.n$CP[j]
# Get the tree for the best model
fit.best <- prune(fit.n,cp=cp)
rpart.plot(fit.best,extra = 101)

Binary Outcome: Pima Indians Diabetes

Next, we classify diabetes status using the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset.

data(PimaIndiansDiabetes2, package = "mlbench")
bin_df <- na.omit(PimaIndiansDiabetes2)
head(bin_df)

Distribution of outcome by candidate predictors

ggplot(bin_df, aes(x = diabetes, y = glucose)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Glucose by Diabetes Status")

ggplot(bin_df, aes(x = diabetes, y = age)) + geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Age by Diabetes Status")

Fit CART with CV to select CP

set.seed(735)
train_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv", 
  number = 10, 
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary)

cart_class <- train(diabetes ~ ., data = bin_df, method = "rpart",
                    trControl = train_control,
                    metric = "ROC",
                    tuneLength = 10)
cart_class
## CART 
## 
## 392 samples
##   8 predictor
##   2 classes: 'neg', 'pos' 
## 
## No pre-processing
## Resampling: Cross-Validated (10 fold) 
## Summary of sample sizes: 353, 353, 353, 353, 352, 353, ... 
## Resampling results across tuning parameters:
## 
##   cp          ROC        Sens       Spec     
##   0.00000000  0.8128041  0.8544160  0.6153846
##   0.03162393  0.7706443  0.8273504  0.6769231
##   0.06324786  0.7586621  0.8311966  0.6615385
##   0.09487179  0.7533092  0.7933048  0.6923077
##   0.12649573  0.7524217  0.7817664  0.7230769
##   0.15811966  0.7524217  0.7817664  0.7230769
##   0.18974359  0.7524217  0.7817664  0.7230769
##   0.22136752  0.7524217  0.7817664  0.7230769
##   0.25299145  0.7524217  0.7817664  0.7230769
##   0.28461538  0.6442308  0.8346154  0.4538462
## 
## ROC was used to select the optimal model using the largest value.
## The final value used for the model was cp = 0.

Code Explanation

  • train() is from the caret package and is a wrapper for fitting models with built-in resampling.
  • diabetes ~ . means we’re predicting the diabetes variable using all other variables (.).
  • method = "rpart" tells caret to fit a classification tree using the rpart package.
  • trainControl()sets how the resampling is done:
  • method = "cv" → perform cross-validation.
  • number = 10→ 10 folds.
  • classProbs = TRUE → compute class probabilities (not just predicted classes).
  • summaryFunction = twoClassSummary → calculate metrics like ROC AUC, sensitivity, specificity.
  • metric = "ROC" tells caret to optimize the model based on ROC AUC.
  • tuneLength = 10 → caret will try 10 different values of the complexity parameter (cp) for the tree, then pick the one with the best AUC.

So, this code finds the “best” CART tree for the Pima data, based on cross-validated ROC AUC.

Final CART tree

best_tree_class <- cart_class$finalModel
rpart.plot(best_tree_class, main = "CART Classification Tree", extra = 101)

⸻

Compare CART vs Naive Bayes for Pima Indians Diabetes

Naive Bayes model

Here, we are going to fit the Naive Bayes model with the naivebayes package.

set.seed(735)
nb_model <- train(diabetes ~ ., data = bin_df, method = "naive_bayes",
                  trControl = train_control,
                  metric = "ROC")
nb_model
## Naive Bayes 
## 
## 392 samples
##   8 predictor
##   2 classes: 'neg', 'pos' 
## 
## No pre-processing
## Resampling: Cross-Validated (10 fold) 
## Summary of sample sizes: 353, 353, 353, 353, 352, 353, ... 
## Resampling results across tuning parameters:
## 
##   usekernel  ROC        Sens       Spec     
##   FALSE      0.8345387  0.8279202  0.6384615
##    TRUE      0.8390423  0.8008547  0.6692308
## 
## Tuning parameter 'laplace' was held constant at a value of 0
## Tuning
##  parameter 'adjust' was held constant at a value of 1
## ROC was used to select the optimal model using the largest value.
## The final values used for the model were laplace = 0, usekernel = TRUE
##  and adjust = 1.

Naive Bayes here will try different internal settings (like kernel estimation for continuous predictors, Laplace smoothing, etc.), then choose the best one using cross-validation.

Code Explanation

• Very similar to the CART example, but method = "naive_bayes" tells caret to use a Naive Bayes classifier (via the naivebayes package).

• Again, it uses the same cross-validation settings (train_control).

• metric = "ROC" means caret will pick the tuning parameter values that maximize the ROC AUC.

Compare ROC AUC

results <- resamples(list(CART = cart_class, NB = nb_model))

Code Explanation

• resamples() is a caret function that takes multiple fitted caret models (here cart_class and nb_model) and extracts the resampling results (cross-validation scores).

• list(CART = cart_class, NB = nb_model) names each model so they can be compared side by side.

summary(results)

bwplot(results, main = "CART vs Naive Bayes")

⸻

Key Takeaways

• CART flexibly partitions the predictor space for continuous or binary outcomes.

• Cross-validation is essential for tuning tree complexity (cp).

• CART trees are interpretable but may not always perform as well as other classifiers.

• Naive Bayes provides a useful baseline for classification problems and often complements CART in comparison.
